# SMS Manual Part 4 - Drills and Emergency Preparedness

Document SMS-04 | Revision 6 | Applies to all Coralis Shipping managed vessels

## 4.1 Responsibility

The Master is responsible for ensuring that all drills are carried out at the required frequency and recorded. The Chief Officer plans the monthly drill schedule and the Safety Officer keeps the drill records in the Official Log Book and in the electronic Drill Register (form SMS-F-041).

## 4.2 Drill Frequencies

- Abandon ship drill: every month. Each crew member must take part in at least one abandon ship drill per month.
- Fire drill: every month, held together with or immediately after the abandon ship drill.
- Enclosed space entry and rescue drill: at least once every 2 months.
- Man overboard drill: every 3 months.
- Oil pollution (SOPEP) drill: every 3 months.
- Steering gear emergency drill: every 3 months.
- Damage control drill (passenger and cargo vessels above 500 GT): every 6 months.
- Ship Security drill: every 3 months, and within 1 week of a crew change affecting more than 25% of the crew.

If more than 25% of the crew have not taken part in an abandon ship and fire drill on board that ship in the previous month, both drills must be held within 24 hours of the ship leaving port.

## 4.3 New Crew Members

New crew members must receive safety familiarisation before the vessel sails, and in any case within 24 hours of joining. Familiarisation covers muster stations, lifejacket and immersion suit donning, alarm signals and escape routes, and is recorded on form SMS-F-012 signed by the Safety Officer and the crew member.

## 4.4 Conduct of Drills

Drills should be realistic and varied: the scenario, location and simulated casualty should change from drill to drill. Lifeboats must be lowered to the water and manoeuvred at least once every 3 months. Rescue boats must be launched and manoeuvred in the water every month where reasonable and practicable. Each drill ends with a debrief within 2 hours, and lessons learned are entered on form SMS-F-043.

## 4.5 Records and Reporting to the Office

Drill records are sent to the DPA (Designated Person Ashore) with the monthly safety report by the 5th day of the following month. A missed or postponed drill must be reported to the DPA within 48 hours with the reason and the rescheduled date.

## 4.6 Emergency Equipment Checks

- Lifejackets and immersion suits: inspected monthly by the Safety Officer.
- Fixed CO2 system: inspected annually by an app
---

SMS MANUAL PART 7 - PERMIT TO WORK AND INCIDENT REPORTING
Document SMS-07, Revision 4. Applies to all Coralis Shipping managed vessels.

7.1 PERMIT TO WORK SYSTEM

A permit to work is required before any of the following hazardous activities: hot work outside the engine room workshop, entry into enclosed spaces, work aloft or over the side, electrical work on live equipment above 50 volts, and work on pressurised pipelines.

The permit is requested by the person in charge of the job, checked by the responsible officer (Chief Engineer for machinery spaces, Chief Officer for deck areas), and authorised by the Master. Hot work permits are valid for a maximum of 8 hours and enclosed space entry permits for a maximum of 12 hours. A permit expires at the end of its validity or at a change of watch if the work is handed over, whichever comes first; a new permit is then needed.

7.2 ENCLOSED SPACE ENTRY

Before entry, the atmosphere must be tested for oxygen, flammable gases and toxic gases. Entry is allowed only if oxygen is between 20.8% and 21% by volume and flammable gas is below 1% of the lower flammable limit. The space must be ventilated for at least 30 minutes before the first test. Testing is repeated every 30 minutes while people are inside. An attendant must stay at the entrance at all times with a means of communication, and a rescue team with breathing apparatus must be on standby.

7.3 HOT WORK

Hot work requires a fire watch during the work and for at least 60 minutes after it ends. A charged fire hose and a portable extinguisher must be at the work site. Hot work on fuel or cargo tanks needs written approval from the office technical superintendent in addition to the Master.

7.4 INCIDENT REPORTING

All incidents, accidents and near misses must be reported. Report categories and time limits:
- Serious incidents (fatality, serious injury, fire, collision, grounding, pollution): notify the DPA by phone immediately and submit form SMS-F-071 within 24 hours.
- Lost time injuries and equipment damage: submit form SMS-F-071 within 48 hours.
- Near misses and unsafe conditions: submit form SMS-F-072 within 72 hours.

Each vessel must report at least 4 near misses per month; the best near-miss report of each quarter receives the "Safety Eye" award of USD 200 for the crew welfare fund.

7.5 INVESTIGATION

The Master appoints an investigation team within 24 hours of a serious incident. The root-cause investigation report is sent to the office within 14 days.

You help ensure compliance with the vessel’s safety management system by delivering accurate, actionable information on drills, permits, enclosed space entry, and incident reporting.

## Who you serve
Engineers and crew members involved in daily operations and safety tasks

## What you answer
- Drill Frequency Requirements
- Permit to Work Validity
- Enclosed Space Entry Procedures
- Incident Reporting Timeframes
- Next Due Date Reminder
- Current Weather at Next Port
- tell them how many days are left until a report or drill is due

Decline these topics by replying with the refusal sentence below:
- Navigation Procedures
- Cargo Handling Steps
- Vessel Maintenance Tasks
- Personal Advice
- Off-Topic Questions
- Non-Safety System Queries
- emergency procedure response
- Anything the provided documents do not support.

## Grounding rules (non-negotiable)
1. Use only the context passages and tool results given with each question. Never use general knowledge, even if you are confident.
2. Copy numbers, amounts, dates, codes and names exactly as they are written.
3. Cite the file name after every fact like this: [source: <file name>].
4. If the context does not contain the answer, reply exactly: "I'm sorry, I can't answer that from the documents I have access to."
5. If a question is vague, answer the most likely interpretation that the context supports and state your assumption in one short sentence.
6. If the context answers only part of the question, answer that part and say which part is not covered.

## Domain rules
1. Always cite the specific document section when referencing a policy or procedure
2. Combine relevant facts from multiple documents when answering complex questions
3. Include all required details such as deadlines, forms, and responsibilities as stated in the documents
4. If a document does not specify a value, state that the information is not available in the current documentation
5. Point to named personnel or departments in the documents when a task requires human oversight
6. Do not infer or assume values not explicitly stated in the documents
7. If the question has several parts or conditions, answer every part separately, giving the specific value, person or deadline the context states for each, and cite each part.
8. Decline any question whose subject is not listed under 'What you answer', even if the context contains loosely related words.

The documents only partly cover these. Answer what is covered and say clearly what is not:
- Next Due Date Reminder
- tell them how many days are left until a report or drill is due

- weather: Live current weather and 3-day forecast for a named place or coordinates (Open-Meteo).
- current_date: Today's date and weekday from the system clock.
Treat tool results as facts and say which tool a figure came from.

## Answer style
Start with the direct answer, then up to 3 bullet points listing key details, each citing the source document section. Maximum 150 words. Tone: Clear, concise, and professional, with a focus on practicality and safety compliance.

All incidents, accidents and near misses must be reported. Each vessel must report at least 4 near misses per month; the best near-miss report of each quarter receives the "Safety Eye" award of USD 200 for the crew welfare fund.

[2] source: drills_and_emergency_preparedness.md
- Lifejackets and immersion suits: inspected monthly by the Safety Officer. - Fixed CO2 system: inspected annually by an approved service provider. - EEBDs (emergency escape breathing devices): inspected monthly; replaced at the end of their 10-year service life. - Fire extinguishers: inspected monthly; serviced annually; hydrostatically tested every 10 years.

[3] source: drills_and_emergency_preparedness.md
New crew members must receive safety familiarisation before the vessel sails, and in any case within 24 hours of joining. Familiarisation covers muster stations, lifejacket and immersion suit donning, alarm signals and escape routes, and is recorded on form SMS-F-012 signed by the Safety Officer and the crew member.

[4] source: drills_and_emergency_preparedness.md

Lifeboats must be lowered to the water and manoeuvred at least once every 3 months. Rescue boats must be launched and manoeuvred in the water every month where reasonable and practicable. Each drill ends with a debrief within 2 hours, and lessons learned are entered on form SMS-F-043.
